extracted.intended_audience: UAI 2017 paper reviewers / program committee members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing submissions to the UAI 2017 conference: what to include in written reviews, how to assess key dimensions (novelty, technical quality, impact, writing), and how to apply the numeric and confidence scoring systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should address both the strengths and weaknesses of the paper - identify the areas where you believe the paper is particularly strong and particularly weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify strong and weak areas; this information is valuable to program chairs and the SPC. Provide precise, not vague, comments and constructive suggestions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain in your own words what is the problem the paper is trying to address, and by what approach. In what area lie the main accomplishments of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optionally include a summary of your opinion, impact and significance. Summaries help clarify the reviewer's understanding and indicate whether central parts of the paper were understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty: 'This is arguably the single most important criterion for selecting papers for the conference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward genuinely new ideas that depart from the 'natural' next step. Assess novelty in context of the problem/application area. Authors should explicitly point out how their work is novel relative to prior work; reviewers should not be required to infer novelty. Consider whether ideas are truly new, novel combinations, adaptations, or extensions of existing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results technically sound? Are there obvious flaws in the conceptual approach? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for ignorance of highly relevant prior work, whether experiments are well thought out and convincing, and whether there are obvious missing experiments. Consider replicability: will others be able to replicate results? Are data sets/code publicly available? Is the evaluation appropriate? Did the authors discuss sensitivity to parameter settings? Did the authors clearly assess both strengths and weaknesses of their approach?

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Impact and Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this really a significant advance in the state of the art? Is this a paper that people are likely to read and cite in later years?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper addresses an important problem (including problems recognizable outside UAI), whether it raises new research issues for the community, whether it is likely to have lasting impact or be useful to researchers/practitioners 5–10 years from now, and whether the work can be built on by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper clearly written? Does it adequately inform the reader? Is there a good use of examples and figures? Is it well organized?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score across the range to identify poorly-written papers. Check for problems with style, grammar, typos, formatting, and references. It is the authors' responsibility to write clearly; reviewers should not be expected to extract information from poor prose. Because there's little time for camera-ready fixes, consider advising revision rather than accepting a poorly-written paper; if likely to accept, provide suggestions and detailed typos to help the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Comments to the Authors (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional free-form section to add comments that don't fit other headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this for extra guidance to authors, clarifications, or suggestions not covered by standard sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Comments to SPC and Chairs (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional confidential section for comments intended only for the SPC and program chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include remarks you do not wish authors to see; in particular, you can include rankings or comparisons among the papers you have reviewed for UAI.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Advice on Review Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as precise as you can in your comments to the authors and avoid vague statements. Your criticism should be constructive where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If giving a low score, be clear about actions authors could take to improve (e.g., cite specific prior work). If experiments are unrealistic or insufficient, suggest remedies (more realistic data sets, larger data sets, different evaluation metrics, sensitivity analyses, etc.). Provide precise citations for claimed prior work; make critiques actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric Scoring (10-point system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 10-point scoring system; reviewers are strongly encouraged to use the full range of scores and not bunch scores in the middle of the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score meanings: 10 = Top 5% of accepted papers, seminal paper; 9 = Top 15% of accepted papers, strong accept; 8 = Top 50% of accepted papers, clear accept; 7 = Good paper, accept; 6 = Marginally above acceptance threshold; 5 = Marginally below acceptance threshold; 4 = Ok but not good enough - rejection; 3 = Clear rejection; 2 = Strong rejection; 1 = Trivial or wrong. Use proceedings from recent UAI conferences to help calibrate your scores. The numeric scores are a vehicle to express evaluation in addition to the in-depth written review and not to supplant it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence Scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Score your confidence in the evaluation using a five-level scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levels: (1) The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature. (2) The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct. (3) The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct. (4) The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper. (5) The reviewer's evaluation is an educated guess.
